hidden_inputs_accounted_for: Real finite-dimensional square matrices and Euclidean norm; reverse triangle inequality and scalar norm formulas.
A zero kernel implies invertibility in finite dimension; invertibility implies a nonzero determinant.
The affine matrix path and its determinant are continuous; a real interval is connected, equivalently the intermediate value theorem prevents a nonzero determinant from changing sign.
Determinant product, scalar scaling, transpose invariance, and determinant of identity.
Principal nonnegative real square root, nonzero positive powers of 2, and elementary real arithmetic.

critical_steps.check: B^T B=(a^2+b^2)I-ab(O+O^T); s^2=kappa gives (a^2+b^2)/4=(kappa+1)/2 and ab/4=(kappa-1)/4.

The 2||v|| lower bound forces kernel zero for all t in [0,b]. det(B_0)=a^n>0; continuity and nonvanishing throughout the interval force det(B_b)>0. Positivity is not inferred from orthogonality of O or from Eq16 alone.

Eq16 gives det(A)=4^(-n)det(B)^2 and therefore initially sqrt(det(A))=2^(-n)|det(B)|. The endpoint sign just proved removes the absolute value. No extra positive-definiteness theorem or Gaussian integral is needed.
Choose left multiplication: O^T B=a O^T-bI using O^T O=I. Then det(O^T B)=det(O^T)det(B)=det(O)det(B). This works for both determinant components and uses no division by det(O).
(a O^T-bI)^T=aO-bI, since the scalars are real and I^T=I. Determinant is invariant under transpose; symmetry of O is not required.
